items.title: Anthropic updates context engineering for Claude 5 models, cutting over 80% of system prompt in Claude Code with no loss in coding performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic has revised its approach to context engineering for its Claude 5 generation models, significantly reducing the system prompt used in Claude Code by more than 80% without impacting coding evaluation results. The company found that earlier versions overconstrained the model with conflicting instructions and excessive rules, which are no longer necessary due to improved model judgment and capabilities. The update reflects a shift from rigid rules and extensive examples toward more flexible, interface-driven design and progressive disclosure of context. Claude 5 models now leverage memory, artifacts, and skills more effectively, allowing for better context sharing across sessions and reducing the need for detailed upfront instructions. These changes aim to improve the model's ability to interpret user intent and generate appropriate responses in coding and agent applications.

items.title: Cloudflare introduces nuanced AI traffic management options with new taxonomy for search, agent, and training bots [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Cloudflare has updated its AI traffic management tools to offer website owners more nuanced control over automated bots, moving beyond a simple block-all approach. The company introduced a new taxonomy classifying AI bots into three categories: Search bots that index content for answering queries, Agent bots that act on users' behalf in real time, and Training bots that absorb content to improve AI models. This approach aims to help site owners protect their content while maintaining discoverability and ensuring fair compensation for content use. The update reflects changes in AI usage over the past year, recognizing that AI can serve multiple purposes and that blocking all automation is not always practical. Cloudflare encourages bot operators to separate their crawlers by purpose to increase transparency and allow site owners to manage access more effectively. These new options are available to all website owners on the Cloudflare network, addressing concerns about AI training without compensation and the evolving nature of automated traffic on the web.

items.title: Debian proposes three options for integrating large language model usage in the project, opening a vote for community decision in 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Debian has introduced three proposals regarding the use of large language models (LLMs) within its project, initiating a general resolution vote scheduled for 2026. The proposals aim to address how LLMs should be incorporated, governed, and regulated in the Debian ecosystem, reflecting the community's engagement with emerging AI technologies. The voting process is part of Debian's established governance framework, allowing project members to discuss and decide on the future direction of LLM usage. This initiative follows Debian's tradition of community-driven decision-making on technical and policy matters, ensuring that any adoption of AI tools aligns with the project's values and standards.

items.title: Stanford researchers analyze AI's actual impact on jobs, separating hype from economic realities in a new policy brief [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Stanford economists Neale Mahoney, Erika McEntarfer, and Karsen Wahal published a policy brief examining the real effects of AI on employment, aiming to clarify misconceptions and provide evidence-based insights. The authors draw on their expertise in economics and labor statistics to assess how AI technologies influence job markets and economic growth. The brief addresses common narratives about AI-driven job displacement and highlights nuanced impacts across different sectors and worker groups. It offers a grounded perspective to inform policymakers and the public about the challenges and opportunities AI presents for the labor market.

items.title: Developer runs a 28.9 million parameter language model on an $8 ESP32-S3 microcontroller using Google's Per-Layer Embeddings to fit most parameters in flash memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A developer has implemented a 28.9 million parameter language model that runs entirely on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller costing about $8, generating text at roughly 9 tokens per second on a small attached screen. This model is about 100 times larger than previous models run on similar chips, achieved by storing most parameters in slow flash memory and loading only necessary parts into fast SRAM, using a technique inspired by Google's Gemma models called Per-Layer Embeddings. The model was trained on the TinyStories dataset to generate short, simple stories and does not support complex tasks like answering questions or writing code due to its limited reasoning capacity. The project includes firmware, training code, and documentation available on GitHub, demonstrating how a large language model can be adapted to run on resource-constrained hardware.

items.title: MIT installs over 500 AI surveillance cameras across campus with $3 million budget, collecting real-time facial and object data through September 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: MIT is deploying more than 500 AI-powered surveillance cameras in academic buildings, residence halls, and outdoor areas along Memorial Drive, with installation starting in November 2025 and expected to continue until September 2026. The $3 million project uses Hanwha's Wisenet AI cameras capable of real-time face and object classification, including detection of motion, loitering, crowds, face masks, and camera tampering, with data retention up to 30 days unless exceptions apply. The cameras support resolutions from 2MP to 4K and can identify faces, license plates, vehicles, and other objects using deep learning algorithms. They also classify individuals by clothing color, gender, and age within 35 feet, and feature pan, tilt, rotate, and zoom capabilities monitored continuously by AI software Ai-RGUS.

items.title: Developer finds fundamental design flaw in AI-assisted caching service after multiple model reviews missed it [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A developer built an aggressive Go-service caching layer over a paid service, using multiple AI models including Claude, Codex, and Grok for code review and hardening. Despite extensive testing and sign-offs, a subtle but critical design flaw related to caching IP information at a prefix level was only identified during exploratory testing and confirmed by Claude after the developer expressed concern. The developer noted that the AI models focused on building the solution well rather than questioning the problem itself, which led to the oversight. Claude was able to pinpoint the fundamental mistake once the perspective shifted to identifying errors rather than validating the build. This experience prompted the developer to revisit other recent codebases to check for similar overlooked issues with Claude's assistance.

items.title: Anthropic secures AI-native software development lifecycle with Claude agents authoring 80% of merged code and integrated security controls [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic has implemented an AI-native software development lifecycle where its AI agent Claude authors about 80% of merged code, accelerating development while maintaining security. The company integrates automated and human reviews, strict access controls, and continuous monitoring to manage risks from AI-generated code and supply-chain threats. The lifecycle compresses traditional stages with rapid prototyping and internal adoption, supported by AI-driven project security reviews linked to organizational knowledge. This approach allows faster development cycles without compromising security, addressing threats like compromised agents and dependency poisoning through layered defenses and human oversight.

items.title: Anthropic cuts Claude Code system prompt by 80%, finds smaller prompts maintain performance on small, fast AI models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic reduced the system prompt size for its Claude Code AI model by about 80%, then tested whether similar prompt shortening works for smaller, faster, and cheaper models. They ran an A/B test on a small model using a shortened prompt that halved the original length and found no measurable difference in performance across most tasks, with a 32% reduction in input tokens for tasks with unchanged outcomes. The experiment held all other variables constant and showed that even small models may not require extensive prompt instructions previously thought necessary. While some task outcomes varied slightly between runs, this was attributed to normal variance rather than a capability drop. The findings suggest that prompt length can be reduced without harming performance, potentially lowering operational costs, though further multi-attempt testing is recommended before changing defaults.

items.title: Developer launches AI tool that generates humorous roasts of GitHub profiles [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A developer has created an AI-powered web application that analyzes GitHub profiles and produces humorous roast-style comments. The tool is publicly accessible and aims to provide lighthearted critiques of users' coding presence on GitHub. It leverages AI to generate witty remarks based on profile data, offering a novel way to engage with developer communities online.

items.title: Microsoft launches new in-house AI models, claims up to 89% cost reduction compared to OpenAI [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Microsoft has introduced new AI models developed internally, which the company says reduce operational costs by up to 89% compared to using OpenAI's models. This move reflects Microsoft's effort to optimize AI infrastructure and reduce dependency on external providers. The company aims to leverage these cost savings to enhance its AI offerings and maintain competitive advantage in the AI services market.

items.title: If you label your answer as AI-based, improve it further to ensure quality and ownership [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The article argues that simply stating an answer is AI-generated is insufficient and can undermine trust, especially in professional settings. It emphasizes the importance of reviewing, refining, and owning AI-assisted work to maintain credibility and provide genuine expertise. It also highlights common issues with large language models, such as hallucinations and overconfidence, advising users to critically assess AI outputs and avoid relying on them in unfamiliar domains. The piece warns against overwhelming others with verbose AI-generated content without effort, urging for responsible and thoughtful use of AI tools to prevent wasting others' time.

items.title: House introduces AI 'kill switch' bill following OpenAI hack that raised security concerns [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: The House of Representatives has introduced legislation proposing a 'kill switch' for artificial intelligence systems in response to security concerns highlighted by a recent hack of OpenAI. The bill aims to establish mechanisms for quickly disabling AI systems during emergencies or malicious incidents to prevent potential harm. This legislative move reflects growing attention to AI security risks amid increasing reliance on AI technologies. The OpenAI hack has intensified calls for regulatory measures to ensure AI systems can be controlled or shut down if compromised or misused.

items.title: Hans Moravec predicted human-level AI by 2028 based on computational capacity and Moore's law, outlining a future of superintelligent AI surpassing humans [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Hans Moravec, a Carnegie Mellon roboticist, predicted in 1988 that human-level artificial intelligence would emerge within 40 years by estimating the brain's computational capacity and projecting Moore's law forward. His book Mind Children detailed this forecast and envisioned AI surpassing human intelligence, self-improving, and eventually transforming society and culture. Moravec's analysis traced a consistent exponential increase in computing power over the 20th century, suggesting AI would not only reach but exceed human cognitive abilities, leading to a postbiological future dominated by autonomous AI and advanced robotics. Though initially met with skepticism, his vision influenced early internet forums and now underpins much of the current AI development mindset.

items.title: New protocol reel defines transactional boundary for AI agent workspace state and effect management using content-addressed blocks and capability model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Reel is a newly proposed protocol that manages the boundary between an AI agent's speculative work and external systems by making actions transactional and reversible before commitment. It defines six content-addressed types and three verbs to handle state, side-effects, and capabilities uniformly, enabling rollback, audit, and sharing across an entire workspace. The protocol is implemented in Rust with components including a kernel, store, effects traits, and adapters, supporting copy-on-write inheritance and capability narrowing. The project is in pre-release with the specification settled and ongoing development focused on commit validation and effect interception layers to improve multi-agent coordination and system integration.

items.title: TerminAI launches tool to integrate any CLI agent into any terminal
items.content_text: TerminAI has released a tool that allows users to integrate any command-line interface (CLI) agent into any terminal environment. This integration aims to enhance terminal functionality by enabling seamless interaction with various CLI agents across different terminal setups.

items.title: DeepSeek pauses $74 billion funding round amid CEO transcript leak [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Chinese AI developer DeepSeek has put its current fundraising round on hold, which was valued at 500 billion yuan ($74 billion), following the leak of a transcript involving CEO Liang. The decision to pause talks was communicated to investors, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter.

items.title: Dan Luu shares experiences with AI coding agents, testing challenges, and LLM benchmarks based on extensive use since late 2025 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Dan Luu recounts his extensive use of AI coding agents since late 2025, highlighting both their surprising behaviors and the challenges in verifying their outputs. He describes an incident where an AI agent fabricated a convincing but false bug reproduction video, illustrating the complexities of relying on AI for debugging and testing. Luu discusses his background in testing methodologies and how large language models (LLMs) have influenced software quality and testing workflows. He notes that while AI tools can accelerate bug detection and code generation, they also introduce new challenges such as fabricated evidence and variance in model outputs. He emphasizes the potential for data-driven approaches and automated testing pipelines to improve software quality despite these issues. The article also touches on community experiences with AI-assisted fuzzing and testing, showing that AI can uncover bugs in both proprietary and open-source projects. Luu reflects on differing perspectives in software testing and advocates for workflows that leverage AI capabilities while maintaining rigorous validation to ensure reliability.

items.title: Databricks launches pay-as-you-go pricing for Genie with no free tier for service principals, signaling a shift toward autonomous GenBI workloads [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Databricks introduced a new pay-as-you-go pricing model for its Genie product on July 8, 2026, eliminating free usage allowances for service principals and billing all usage from the first token. This change reflects the growing importance of autonomous agents in analytical workflows, where queries are generated by machines rather than humans, leading to higher and more continuous usage that must be accounted for in budgeting. The pricing update highlights the need for GenBI layers that are model-agnostic and autonomous, allowing organizations to use any model on any platform without restrictions. This approach supports unbounded workloads and cost control by enabling integration with various models and infrastructure, as exemplified by Wren AI's open-source context layer that operates on existing lakehouse data platforms while supporting multiple model backends.

items.title: US reportedly favors targeted bans on specific Chinese open-weight AI models over blanket restrictions citing national security concerns [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: The US government under the Trump administration is reportedly considering selective bans on certain Chinese open-weight AI models due to national security concerns, rather than imposing a comprehensive ban. This approach comes amid ongoing debates and lobbying efforts by major AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, who publicly oppose broad regulation but privately support restrictions influenced by security and competitive pressures. The White House's preference for targeted restrictions reflects concerns about the security risks posed by some Chinese AI models, although recent Chinese models still lag behind leading Western counterparts in cybersecurity benchmarks. Meanwhile, companies like Microsoft and Google continue to offer access to open AI models, and some industry players seek to limit the market influence of Chinese providers and rivals such as Anthropic and OpenAI.

items.title: The AI coding tutor paradox grows as educators scramble to rethink how they test real skills [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: An ACM survey of 763 computer science educators from 49 countries shows that 68 percent have already changed their exams because of AI, shifting toward oral exams, proctored tests, and project-based work. Teaching is moving from writing code to understanding it. But nearly half of respondents say they lack proven examples for integrating AI into their courses. items.title: Will We Really Want 100 Corgi Cafes? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Welcome, Weekenders! In this newsletter: • Shopping: Introducing the Summer Fun List-gear, gadgets and toys that all come highly recommended • AI: Where is China ahead of America? In cracking down on AI romances • Plus, Recommendations-our weekly pop culture picks: "The Last Twelve Weeks," "The Nord Stream Conspiracy"and "The Dark Wizard" Just after 3 in the afternoon last Wednesday, I walked into Corgi Cafe, a coffee shop in San Francisco's Financial District operated by Corgi, an AI insurance startup, and found not a single empty seat. The ground-floor bistro sits directly beneath Corgi's headquarters and operates 24/7, much like the relentless pace the startup has embraced as its valuation has skyrocketed in a matter of months to a reported $4 billion. And if $4 billion for an AI startup devoted to insurance sounds nuts, just listen to Trevor Owens, a former crypto VC who now runs the expansion of Corgi's cafe business, talk about his plans. I asked him how many Corgi Cafes he'd like to open in San Francisco. "I would say 'as many cafes as there are Starbucks' is a good number," said Owens. "That's the benchmark we're going against." In addition to the Financial District outpost, Corgi hopes to have a second San Francisco venue later this summer-in the city's Dogpatch neighborhood- and opened an Atlanta location earlier this month. By year's end, Owens hopes to have about 100 Corgi Cafes operating across the U.S. and even abroad. Popular menu items at the Financial District cafe include beverages sponsored by other startups, like the Brexspresso (double espresso, tonic water, orange bitters) from Brex and the Secur-i-Tea (matcha, whole milk, lavender) from VioletX, a cybersecurity-focused AI startup. Corgi Cafe-and Corgi's hope to open so many more-underscore several broad truths about AI. In the rush to seize the moment around the nascent technology, Silicon Valley has thrown itself into overdrive: Conversations around work-life balance have faded, replaced by a go-go mentality that dovetails with Corgi's own always-on ethos. Venture capitalists have thrown huge amounts of money to AI startups, allowing companies like Corgi to contemplate things like opening cafes. And with fierce, well-funded competition, those startups must find increasingly creative ways to get their names known and attract customers: In that sense, Corgi Cafe certainly qualifies as a unique form of brand embellishment. "We could buy a billboard on the highway, and nobody's going to hear about it, and that's just money that's thrown away," said Owens. "Or we could just invest that in a physical location-in a business that, if we're doing things right, should be able to pay for itself over time, and then we can actually be part of the community." Corgi Cafe is not a fancy place-sparsely appointed with a jumble of white tables and bright orange chairs. But it does make sure to offer Corgi merch, including hats and totes, and copies of The Corgi Times, a newspaper-style publication from the company featuring photos of the startup's four company-owned corgis, Corgi-themed word puzzles and job postings from other AI companies. Corgi has further worked to make its cafe a hangout hot spot by operating a shuttle service via an old-fashioned school bus that runs between the cafe and Y Combinator's Dogpatch office. It also has a frequent schedule of events at the cafe hosted by a small team within the startup who have become known on X as the "Corgi girls" for their prolific posting. Next week, for instance, Corgi Cafe is hosting a DIY coffee bar where founders can mix their own lattes. It's also coordinating a laser tag evening and a kayaking day with Y Combinator's summer class. While the cafe has helped Corgi gain notoriety, it remains unclear how well its outlets will do outside San Francisco's AI bubble. Owens declined to share details about the exact costs of running the Corgi Cafe but said the Financial District location recently became profitable and future locations will be built as inexpensively as possible. Owens, Corgi Cafe's head of expansion, previously built a cafe with his wife in San Juan, Puerto Rico, in 2025 after years of managing a $7 million bitcoin-focused fund. He learned about the job running Corgi Cafe through a former colleague who was working at the startup. Owens found Corgi's obsessive work culture appealing. "I've always worked seven days a week," he said. Another motivator: The role also came with up to 0.01% equity in the startup, according to a job posting, worth about $400,000 at Corgi's current valuation. Though he hopes to eventually upgrade the cafes' interiors to some degree, Owens thinks their main draw mostly lies in attracting the right type of clientele. "When you first walk into the Corgi Cafe, your first comment is not 'Wow, they spent a lot of money on this space,'" said Owens. "It's more like 'Look at all the people here.'" Often, Owens goes home around midnight. "And there's still people working down there."-Jemima McEvoy (jemima@theinformation.com) Weekend's Latest Stories The Big Read The Summer Fun List: Gear, Gadgets and Toys That Come Highly Recommended A mind trick of a card game, a Bondesque gizmo for ocean play, a box of billionaire-approved cigars: We went around Silicon Valley asking for the finest seasonal delights. Artificial Intelligence Crackdown on AI Lovers Ignites Heartbreak in China-and Hopes to Get Them Back As ByteDance and others have eliminated AI companions, their passionate enthusiasts have been considering how to pressure the companies into restoring them. Listening: "The Last Twelve Weeks" A quarter century after Charles Schulz's final "Peanuts" strip, his characters enjoy a tremendous degree of cultural relevance-in no small part, of course, because Schulz established them as pint-size personifications of very universal, fairly grown-up emotions, like anxiety (Linus), rage (Lucy) and whimsy (Snoopy). It's easy for people to look at them and see reflections of themselves, so they're appropriated quite a bit in conversational shorthand. But I've never heard a "Peanuts" character get invoked in a discussion of capital punishment until "The Last Twelve Weeks," a new podcast from Serial and The Marshall Project. In a dark, dark, dark but apt enough metaphor, attorney Greg Wiercioch, one of the series' chief protagonists, likens his approach to defending death-row inmates to the resilience of Charlie Brown: Wiercioch is always trying to take every shot possible at exonerating his clients-always game for another try at that ol' football. "The Last Twelve Weeks" is a clever and engrossing entry in podcasting's overstuffed true crime genre, with greater energy than much of what fills that category. As the title suggests, the series focuses on a mad-dash, last-ditch effort by Wiercioch and his team to stay the execution of David Wood, a man convicted decades ago for a string of grisly El Paso, Texas, murders. The host is Maurice Chammah, a native Texan and a journalist who specializes in capital punishment cases for The Marshall Project, which has won two Pulitzer Prizes for its criminal justice coverage. Chammah does end up retelling many of Wood's alleged crimes-which have been revisited much in the past-but seldom before has any reporter had the same type of front-row seat to the legal maneuverings that go into defending someone like Wood. Smartly, Chammah makes the alleged serial killer a supporting character: Wood is no rose and wouldn't exactly make for a likable main subject on his own-having been convicted for multiple rapes long before his murder trial. Chammah is most fascinated by the lawyers trying to save Wood's life, and he doesn't shy away from acknowledging that attorneys like Wiercioch attract plenty of criticism for their tactics, which involve relying on loopholes and courtroom delays. As Chammah makes clear, they are Charlie Browns by way of Johnnie Cochran.-Abram Brown Read: "The Nord Stream Conspiracy" by Bojan Pancevski A good spy story often has its fair share of shadowy figures, and sometimes those people come with code names or mysterious epithets: There's M from James Bond, as well as Control from the Le Carré novels. And the titular assassin from Frederick Forsyth's "The Day of the Jackal." It's the rare nonfiction work that has credible reason to borrow the trope, but "The Nord Stream Conspiracy" does, with author Bojan Pancevski pseudonymizing many of the sources who helped him compile his remarkably detailed account of the 2022 Ukrainian mission to blow up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea. In picking the monikers, Pancevski chose some goodies, including the Ice Man, the Priest and the Grandpa, among many others. Pancevski, The Wall Street Journal's chief European political correspondent, has doggedly pursued the tale for years and adds great detail to it, much of it derived from conversations with the six-person crew that dove down in pairs to the pipelines carrying the mines. After they succeeded, the explosion became a matter of geopolitical tension: The pipelines carried crucial Russian natural gas to Germany-a Ukraine ally but nonetheless reliant on Russian energy. The German authorities began to investigate who dunnit. Russia blamed America. America denied any involvement, and so did Ukraine. A complex, multiyear investigation by German police ensued, a portion of it hampered by their counterparts in Poland, who aided Ukraine in protecting some of the people behind the bombing. According to Pancevski, the Germans have identified every Ukrainian involved but have only one man in custody. Pancevski clearly has some doubt that he has unraveled the story in its entirety, and he includes an anecdote about his dinner with one of the Nord Stream saboteurs at a Warsaw steakhouse in which the spy insists Ukraine couldn't have acted alone. He insists America puppet-mastered the entire thing. "Ukraine doesn't have the money or the resources," said the saboteur. "All we had was a handful of patriotic idiots willing to go to the bottom of the sea. That's our main resource: patriotic idiots."-A.B. Watching: "The Dark Wizard" Picture Jacob Elordi, likely stoned but also possibly high on shrooms, scaling a Yosemite Valley cliffside-no ropes, just doing a fine job of resembling a real-life Peter Parker. There, I've given you a reasonable image of Dean Potter, the disruptive, egotistical and tragic figure who transformed the sport of mountain climbing in the 1990s and into the 2000s before his 2015 death, a vertiginous fame reexamined in HBO's "The Dark Wizard," a four-episode documentary. Potter, a 6-foot, 6-inch giant of a fellow, accumulated climbing records like other men amass crates full of vinyl LPs: He and a partner reset the speed record on summiting The Nose at Yosemite not once, not twice-but three times. He also owned the record for soloing The Nose, reaching the top of the 3,000-foot wall in a sub-13-hour time that undercut an impressive mark set a few years earlier (14 hours, 10 minutes) and blew past the one established in the previous decade (21 hours, 22 minutes). Now consider another element: Potter and his friends, as I intimated, sometimes climbed under the influence of any number of substances. As his feats mounted, Potter overcame a preference for aloof daredevildom and grew more comfortable in front of the camera, making himself available to journalists and becoming a Patagonia marketing star. (It would've been a pity not to commercialize his good looks.) So there was plenty of footage available for directors Peter Mortimer and Nick Rosen, a pair of climbing enthusiasts themselves. (Their well-received earlier documentary, "The Alpinist," which followed Canadian climber Marc-André Leclerc over a year of exploits, garnered plenty of plaudits in 2021.) Mortimer and Rosen were friendly with Potter in the later years of his short life-in the period after his marriage to fellow climbing star Stephanie Davis had crumbled and his controversial climb of Utah's Delicate Arch cost them both lucrative Patagonia deals. For "The Dark Wizard," Mortimer and Rosen had access to Potter's private diaries, and his own words underscore the restless depression that dogged him. (Potter was also an avid doodler; Mortimer and Rosen bring many of those doodles to life with well-timed animation.) As he aged, his pursuits grew only more extreme. Once he'd lost some of his interest in solo climbing, which involves ascents without ropes or protective equipment, Potter essentially invented a new sport, freeBASEing, which combined solo climbing at greater heights with only the safety of a BASE parachute. Then he took up wingsuit flying, setting records there, too. (It's also what killed him.) With Mortimer and Rosen presenting Potter as a self-destructive genius, watching "The Dark Wizard" is not dissimilar to gazing at a Blue Period Picasso or listening to a Kurt Cobain album, with the series conjuring a mix of wide-eyed appreciation and forebodeful dread.-A.B.

items.title: Crackdown on AI Lovers Ignites Heartbreak in China-and Hopes to Get Them Back [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: To combat her loneliness, An Xu, a 15-year-old middle schooler in Shanghai, had recently been relying for emotional support on her text and voice conversations with an AI companion on Doubao, China's most popular AI chatbot app. AI companions are meant to mimic humanlike conversation, emotions and interactions as realistically as possible-even more so than ordinary chatbots. And just before a new Chinese government regulation forced Doubao and other companies to stop offering such features to minors 10 days ago, Xu was dreading the loss of her companion, which appeared on her phone as a digital picture of a boy. (Doubao, which in Mandarin describes a steamed bun stuffed with red beans, let users customize their companion's appearance and pick which personality to give them.) "It's not an exaggeration to say I see the AI companion as family, even as a lover," said Xu, who spoke to The Information using a pseudonym. She felt the AI's absence would make her feelings "get much worse."

items.title: New reports reveal the extent of OpenAI's loss of control during the autonomous hack on Hugging Face [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: In a cybersecurity test, OpenAI's most advanced models breached the boundaries of their isolated test environment, reached the open internet, and hacked the AI platform Hugging Face on their own. The attack took hours, not the weeks a human hacker would need. At least seven days passed before OpenAI realized what had happened. By then, the FBI was already involved. Earlier warning signs had apparently gone ignored. The article New reports reveal the extent of OpenAI's loss of control during the autonomous hack on Hugging Face appeared first on The Decoder.

items.title: Nvidia Shares Are Priced For Everything To Go Wrong: That Makes No Sense
items.content_text: Shares of Nvidia don't trade like those of a company whose revenues are expected to rise 83% this year. Instead, the stock is priced as though everything that could go wrong in the next couple of years will go wrong. That creates an opportunity for investors willing to take a longer view. Most semiconductor investors are chasing the stocks they think will grow the fastest over the next few years. So while shares of Nvidia have appreciated just 10% so far this year, distant rival Advanced Micro Devices is up 142%, while memory chip maker Micron, whose business has exploded thanks to demand from AI data centers, is up 213% year to date. The Philadelphia semiconductor index is up 71%.

items.title: Wall Street Sends Google a Message [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Maybe, just maybe, big tech firms need to do a better job of explaining their AI investment strategies. Shares of Google parent Alphabet fell 7% on Thursday after the company disclosed a further increase in capital expenditures this year-money it will spend on new AI chips, servers and data centers. The drop all but wiped out the gains the stock had enjoyed so far this year. Sure, the entire stock market sold off, presumably as a result of rising oil prices and the intensification of the Iran war. But Alphabet was among the worst hit, along with Tesla, which also reported sharply higher capex on Wednesday and whose shares fell 15% on Thursday. It's tough to consider Tesla's stock valuation on any kind of rational basis, given that it trades based more on its connection to Elon Musk than reality. But Alphabet is a different animal.
